newsitem.title: USA: Consumers reined in credit-buying in August.
newsitem.headline: Consumers reined in credit-buying in August.

text.p: Consumer buying on credit expanded at the slowest rate during August in more than three years, the Federal Reserve said on Monday, adding to signs of slowing second-half economic activity.
Total instalment credit grew by $3.3 billion at a 3.5 percent annual rate, less than half the revised $7.3 billion increase posted in July, when credit was rising at a 7.6 percent annual rate.
A leveling off in new-car loans in August and an abrupt drop in the rate of credit-card use accounted for the falloff in credit growth.
The last time instalment credit grew more slowly was in May 1993, when debts were paid down by $200 million.
Auto loans increased by only $200 million in August, at a 0.5 percent annual rate, far below July's $2 billion increase when loans were growing at a 6.7 percent annual rate.

Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern trust Co. in Chicago, said that with the economy now into its sixth year of expansion from the 1990-91 recession, many consumers already have bought the new cars and other expensive goods they wanted.

"We're way past the peak of consumer credit growth," Dederick said. But he added: "There's nothing here that is suggesting we're seeing a developing weakness -- just a loss of dynamism in spending that was there earlier."

Most analysts anticipate the economy will slow from an annual growth rate of 4.7 percent in the second quarter to around a 2.5 percent rate in the second half, partly because of less pent-up demand for costly goods.

Revolving, or credit-card, debt also grew much more slowly in August, rising by $2.8 billion at a 7.5 percent annual rate. That was just half the $5.6 billion advance in July, when it was expanding at a 15.2 percent annual rate.
Consumer spending fuels about two-thirds of national economic activity, and any pullback in the rate of spending quickly shows up in weaker growth.

Other credit, a catch-all category that includes consumer bank loans but not real estate mortgages, grew by $400 million at a 1.3 percent annual rate in August after contracting by $300 million at a 1.3 percent rate in July, the Fed said.
